note: Delivery §5a.3 — the canonical, domain-separated registration proof. The signature input is the JCS serialization (RFC 8785) of the object with "sig" omitted; the signature is Ed25519 under "principal". The "v" constant is inside the signed bytes and is the domain tag.
domainTagNote: rltp-carrier-proof/0.3 appears in no other signed artifact of this stack. A verifier MUST reject an object whose v is not byte-equal to this constant. Wire 0.3 (round-36 B-1): every purpose names the queue it acts on, so rkid is present in all four; generation and addressChallenge remain absent in the session-scoped purposes, which change no succession. The /0.2 form was never instantiated outside this repository.
challengeEncoding: exactly 32 raw bytes, canonical unpadded base64url — exactly 43 characters
sigEncoding: Ed25519 over the JCS bytes, carried as canonical base58btc with the z multibase prefix — the same signature encoding and canonicity rule Encounter 2.3 imposes on every signature of this stack

keys.principalSeedNote: the Ed25519 seed of the control principal of identity-derivation.json carrierRelationship case 1 (did:web:carrier.example)
keys.rkidNote: documented sample X25519 keys, sha2-256 of the ASCII labels rltp/vector/carrier-proof/rkid-1 and -2

generationMonotonicity.note: Delivery §5a.3 — a rebind binds only on a STRICTLY HIGHER generation than the one the carrier last accepted. Equal generation with the same principal is registered(idempotent); equal generation with a different principal is refused (the carrier cannot decide a tie the register decides by nonce bytes); lower is refused(stale-generation). This is what stops a device restored from an older backup — which still holds root IKM, the older nonce and the rkid private key, and can therefore prove everything — from rolling the binding back.

cases.case: a restored device presents generation 1 with valid proofs
the same generation, the same principal
the same generation, a DIFFERENT principal — a tie the carrier cannot decide
a genuine rotation: generation 3

equalGenerationTie.note: Delivery §5a.3 / Identity §7a.3 — the composite the two state machines did not cover separately. The register decides an equal-generation race by the smallest nonce bytes; the carrier cannot see them, and this stack carries NO value from which that ordering could be reconstructed — not because such a value is impossible (a carrier-scoped order-preserving map is constructible; the categorical impossibility claim of an earlier casting is withdrawn) but because none is designed: what one would have to satisfy is written down as Delivery §12 DO-7. So refused(stale-generation) at an equal generation is a WAIT STATE, and the healing path is a rotation.

steps.step: the device holding the LARGER nonce reaches the carrier first and binds
the registers merge: the SMALLER nonce is canonical (Identity §7a.3) — the carrier learns nothing of this
the canonical device presents its rebind: equal generation, different principal
it rotates — a FRESH nonce at generation + 1, so the principal is newly derived and differs from both tie candidates

equalGenerationTie.healingCost: exactly one rotation, borne by the honest case that produced the tie
equalGenerationTie.rotationNonceNote: documented sample, deterministic for this vector set (sha2-256 of the ASCII label "rltp/vector/carrier-relationship/nonce-3")

tieAtTheMaximum.note: Delivery §5a.3 / Identity §7a.3 — the doubly theoretical corner: a tie AT the generation maximum, where no rotation is available. The exit is not re-addressing (a holder cannot elect that) but the rule that was already there: entries are superseded, NEVER DELETED, so every device retains the bound entry and can derive its principal. The binding stands and stays collectable; what is lost is only the ability to change which of two principals holds it.
tieAtTheMaximum.why: collection and conclusion require possession of the BOUND principal's key; every device derives it from the retained superseded entry, so deposits arrive, are collected and are concluded
remainingLevers: Identity §7a.2's move to a different configured C (different principals, N untouched)
a genuinely new relationship chain — a social event of the companions, never an instruction

releasedAndReRegistered.note: Delivery §5a.3/§5a.9 — after the two-phase wind-up releases queue and binding, a device from an old backup still holds the older nonce and the rkid private key and can prove everything. The binding tombstone (rkid, highest generation ever accepted) is what keeps a superseded generation from buying NEW authorization past the release. Stated exactly (round-19 M-2): a principal the carrier is still bound to keeps collecting until a strictly higher generation rebinds; what supersession forbids is registering, rebinding and resurrecting..

steps.step: the binding is released at the end of the wind-up
a restored device presents generation 1 with valid proofs
the same device presents generation 2 — equal, not greater
the holder registers afresh at generation 3

releasedAndReRegistered.residual: The tombstone does not expire in time; it leaves in exactly two ways (5a.3): CONSUMED by a registration carrying a strictly greater generation — the released x register/rebind cell, which never keeps it beside the new binding — or EVICTED at the declared max-binding-tombstones bound, where the normative TOTAL ORDER decides: the longest-released tombstone goes first, ties broken by ascending unsigned bytewise order of the decoded rkid key bytes (round-43 B-2: the first 0.65 draft left order and bound to storage policy, which re-opened the round-15/19 divergence — same observable history, different answer to the same old proof). HOW an implementation realizes the order across restarts is its own affair; THAT it holds is conformance. For an evicted rkid the anti-resurrection guarantee ends, and that consequence is reachable only by a party holding BOTH halves — the person or a device holding their state, never a third party.

evictionRule.evicts: the longest-released tombstone; ties broken by ascending unsigned bytewise order of the decoded rkid key bytes. A total order over facts the carrier already holds — release sequence and key bytes — with no prescribed bookkeeping: ordinals, counters or logs are implementation, the ORDER is the promise.
evictionRule.consequenceForEvictedRkid: the anti-resurrection guarantee ends for that address
evictionRule.reachableBy: only a party holding both the principal key and the rkid private key
evictionRule.attackerCostPerTombstone: one full registration per tombstone (both possession proofs, the carrier's own admission gate, its capacity answer). The orphan-horizon waits run in PARALLEL — bindings prepared together release together after ONE horizon — so a carrier that wants a one-wave flush to be expensive declares max-binding-tombstones well above the number of bindings it serves at once.
evictionRule.order: total: release order, oldest first; ties by ascending bytewise rkid key bytes

store.note: Real X25519 multikeys (documented samples). tomb-a and tomb-c release in the SAME sweep, so the bytewise rkid order decides between them — the vector exercises the tie-break as part of the order, not post hoc. The eviction order is DERIVED by the runner from releaseSweep and the decoded key bytes; ordinals and counters are implementation and ship no more (0.65 scope re-cast, round-43 B-2).

recoveryDistance.note: Round-21 B-3: the cost of coming back after the release is not 'one rotation' — it is the generation distance. Derived from the steps above rather than asserted.
recoveryDistance.formula: t - g + 1 rotations of N, where t is the generation the tombstone recorded and g the one the recovered copy carries
recoveryDistance.atTheMaximum: where t is 2^53-1 no generation is strictly greater, so no number of rotations suffices: that address is not re-registrable at that carrier. Identity 7a.3's terminal rule applies and the lever is 7a.2's move to a different configured carrier string.

boundRevision.note: round-45 B-3 — lowering max-binding-tombstones trims the store at the instant the revision takes effect, in one linearized transition, by the same total order. 'Prospective, never retroactive' governs running acts; a store is standing state.

after.why: tomb-a and tomb-c are the longest-released (sweep 1, tie by key bytes) and go in order; the trim is atomic — a carrier that waits for the next release holds a different store than one that trims, after identical histories

carrierEntryLossRecovery.note: round-39 B-1: Identity §9.3 promises that losing the carrier entry ALONE — pair context held, so the rkid private key is held — is replaceable. The lost entry IS {nonce, generation}, so the holder knows neither the old principal nor the generation to exceed. Nothing before this vector executed that path, and executed it fails: a fresh N at generation 1 against a live binding at generation g is refused(stale-generation), not success. The contract now makes the refusal CARRY the held generation, which costs one extra exchange and nothing else. Round-41 M-2/B-3: the first shipping of this vector fixed state=live and generation=4 only, so the categorical 'two exchanges' promise stayed green while the lifecycle makes the count a FUNCTION of the held state. The per-state family below is that function, executed.

steps.why: the holder lost {nonce, generation}; a fresh N can only start at 1
disclosed + 1 — strict monotonicity is an ORDERING rule, and the address challenge is the access rule, which this holder passes

withoutDisclosure.why: the holder can only guess; every guess at or below the held generation is refused identically, and the promise of Identity §9.3 is unkeepable

carrierEntryLossRecovery.disclosureIsNotAnAccessGrant: reaching this verdict already required a signature under the named principal AND the opened address challenge, which only the holder of the rkid private key can produce. That party may rebind at ANY higher generation whether or not it learns the current one, so the number grants nothing it did not already have.

perHeldState.note: how many exchanges the promised replacement costs, by the state the carrier holds for that rkid. The number is a function of the state, not a constant. A return may additionally meet the carrier's retriable capacity refusal; 5a.9's priority rule (a return outranks an arrival) ORDERS that wait — no newcomer is served while the returner waits; nothing promises that room appears, and the practical bound is the plural carrier world (round-46 B-2) — and the third case executes it: capacity refusals are retriable and end when the carrier has room, and no rotation helps or is needed.

cases.why: the carrier holds a record to exceed, and the holder cannot know it without the disclosure
a closing binding is still held, so the generation question is the same one; the return also ends the wind-up (5a.9)

the carrier is at its own limits, so the first answers are registration-refused(capacity) — retriable, not about the generation, and no rotation helps: the holder retries, outranking every new registration (5a.9), and rebinds once the carrier has room
the binding was released and its tombstone evicted, so no record survives to exceed and the fresh N binds at once — the categorical promise was wrong in this direction too
the tombstone carries t=4 and is exactly the record to exceed; the successful registration consumes it

collection.note: purpose=collect: rkid IS present — it names the queue this collection acts on (round-36 B-1: a principal may hold several addresses at one carrier, so resolving the queue through the principal left two conformant carriers free to answer the same bytes differently). addressChallenge and generation remain ABSENT: this act changes no succession, and their absence is part of the JCS bytes.

conclusion.note: round-37 M-2: the fourth purpose, shipped signed. `conclude` names its queue (wire 0.3) and carries neither `generation` nor `addressChallenge` — it ends a session against a binding that already exists and touches no succession.

negatives.note: Each negative changes one value; the JCS bytes therefore differ from the registration bytes and the shipped signature MUST NOT verify over them. This is the executable form of "the proof is not transplantable".

cases.case: transplanted to a second rkid
transplanted to a second carrier
transplanted to a second principal
purpose changed from register to rebind
a foreign domain tag
a challenge replaced
the generation changed

duplicateRule.note: Delivery §5a.5 — two submissions to one queue are duplicates IFF their sealed envelopes are byte-identical (rkid, epk, nonce, ciphertext). A key-blind carrier can compare nothing else. Re-sealing one document yields a fresh epk/nonce/ciphertext and is therefore NOT a duplicate at the carrier; §6.2 absorbs that at the receiver, after decryption, on the document digest.
duplicateRule.metering: A duplicate consumes the admission resource exactly like an admitted submission and consumes NO storage; the check sits after the resource charge and before storage admission, so it can neither bypass the charge nor reach the store.
duplicateRule.retention: The comparison value is held exactly as long as the deposit is held; after conclusion or give-up a byte-identical re-presentation is a NEW submission and is admitted.

cases.case: byte-identical replay of an admitted envelope
the SAME document re-sealed — fresh epk, nonce and ciphertext
identical bytes but a different rkid — a different queue entirely
byte-identical re-presentation AFTER the first deposit was concluded

queueFloorAccounting.note: Delivery §4.4 guarantee 5 — a queue below its declared queue-floor is never refused for global occupancy, and admission is decided on the occupancy AFTER the deposit. The the occupancy-formula these cases were first written against left the protocol in the 0.65 scope re-cast; what the cases execute now is the guarantee itself: growth within the floor cannot be refused for anything global, growth above it can.

cases.case: the round-11 counter-example: A at its floor, B one byte below, a 1-byte deposit to B
cases.why: within the floor, admission depends on nothing global — the guarantee is the promise, and whatever bookkeeping meets it is the carrier's own

cases.case: the same queue one byte above its floor
cases.why: above the floor the room is elastic and globally shared — a refusal there is honest

cases.case: a closing queue holds bytes: it contributes used, not a floor
cases.why: a closing queue admits and counts like a live one (5a.9) — its bytes cannot be handed out twice

crossTrafficMeter.note: round-45 B-1 — guarantee 5 binds s4 in the cross-queue direction: a below-floor submission is refused neither for global occupancy (s6) nor because OTHER queues' traffic drained a meter (s4). The queue's own metering may refuse it, retriably (DO-6: whoever spends a queue's own budget holds its address).

cases.case: below-floor submission while other queues' flood drained the meter
below-floor submission while the queue's OWN traffic drained its meter
above-floor submission while other queues' flood drained the meter
cases.why: above the floor the room and the metering are honestly shared — guarantee 5 draws its line AT the floor

encodingAcceptanceSurface.note: Round-18 B-1. base58btc is not a positional encoding, so — unlike the base64url challenges, where six bits per character let a pattern forbid a non-canonical alias outright — no pattern in the shipped JSON-Schema dialect can require a DECODED multicodec prefix or a DECODED byte length. These six values ALL satisfy carrier-proof.schema.json and are ALL invalid per Delivery §5a.3. They are shipped so that an implementation which stops at schema validation is detected rather than assumed absent.
encodingAcceptanceSurface.rule: A carrier MUST decode before any other check: principal = did:key: + z over 0xed 0x01 || 32 bytes; rkid = z over 0xec 0x01 || 32 bytes; sig = z over exactly 64 bytes. Anything else is refused(malformed).
encodingAcceptanceSurface.whyLengthCannotDecide: A leading zero byte encodes as '1', so the achievable base58btc length envelope of a 64-byte value runs from 64 (all zero) to 88, and it OVERLAPS those of 63- and 65-byte values. The previous pattern {86,88} was therefore wrong in both directions: it accepted 63 and 65 bytes and rejected a legitimate 64-byte signature with three leading zero bytes.

cases.why: the z6Mk text lead does not prove the decoded multicodec: this decodes to 0xec 0xfe, not Ed25519 0xed 0x01
decodes to 0xed 0x02 — the second prefix byte is not 0x01
decodes to 0xeb 0xfe, not X25519 0xec 0x01
decodes to 0xec 0x02 — the second prefix byte is not 0x01
86 base58btc characters decode to 63 bytes; §5a.3 requires exactly 64
88 base58btc characters decode to 65 bytes; §5a.3 requires exactly 64

encodingAcceptanceSurface.positiveControl: The shipped registration proof decodes correctly on all three fields; the runner checks that too, so the negative check cannot pass by rejecting everything.

bindingLifecycle.note: Delivery §5a.3 — the queue-binding lifecycle as ONE total machine, cast in round 22 after three rounds found corners of it by composition. This block is the executable form of the normative table: the runner enumerates the whole (state x input x guard) domain and requires exactly one cell per point. 0.67: the two-step wind-up (give-up-sweep, then release) is merged into the single deadline transition of Delivery 0.66 (round-43 B-1 / round-44 M-1) — the vector executes the table the spec actually casts.

guards.gt: g' > the recorded generation (g in live/closing, t in released)

bindingLifecycle.invariant: an rkid is in exactly one state, and the tombstone store holds exactly the rkids in `released` — which is what makes the k-counting of the release step right
bindingLifecycle.entryCondition: the table is entered only by a request that passed §4.4 step (b) and both possession proofs; malformed, possession-failed, capacity and admission-resource are decided before the state is consulted. A submission is not an input here — it runs §5a.5's outcome set.
bindingLifecycle.purposeRule: `purpose` does not select a cell: register and rebind are distinct in the signed bytes and equivalent in effect. A carrier MUST NOT refuse a proof because its purpose disagrees with the state it finds.

cells.note: no recorded generation exists, so no comparison applies: a first registration is accepted at any generation in the domain
round-22 B-2: this holds whether or not P' = P; the recorded generation advances to g'
the binding returns to live and admission reopens (§5a.9)

cells.why: one linearized transition (round-43 B-1): every inherited life has ended at or before the deadline, so everything is given up and the binding releases in the same step; a tombstone (rkid, g) is created

cells.note: round-22 B-1: the tombstone is CONSUMED — its store entry goes with it; it is not kept beside the new binding
the anti-resurrection guarantee for this rkid ends

findingCases.why: neither kept beside the binding nor evicted; the only proof that consumes it is one the tombstone already permits

findingCases.case: round-22 B-2 higher generation, same principal
findingCases.why: the outcome names the succession, not a change of person; the recorded generation MUST advance

findingCases.case: round-22 B-3 purpose does not select a cell
findingCases.why: a holder recovering from a partial loss cannot know the carrier's state; §5a.9's return path depends on its guess not mattering

bindingLifecycle.algebraNote: Round-23 B-2: every cell of this table draws its outcome from ONE closed set — the verdicts a presenter is told, plus the internal transitions that have no presenter. A cell naming anything else is nonconformant, and so is a verdict outside the list.

capacityRule.note: 0.65: registration-refused(capacity) is a carrier resource answer (4.4 guarantee 2) — retriable, deterministic in the carrier's own state, never about the presenter. Two port-observable rules bound it: a request for a binding the carrier holds is never refused because traffic for unknown addresses exhausted something (guarantee 4), and a return outranks an arrival (5a.9).

counterExample.why: a rebind of a held binding is the honest return path; refusing it for a limit that new bindings exhausted would breach guarantee 4

generationSpelling.note: Round-28 M-1, corrected in round 29: the canonical decimal form of `generation` (Identity §7a.3) must be checked on the RECEIVED BYTES. Two of these lexemes are not valid JSON numbers at all and die in the parser; the other two parse, satisfy the schema, canonicalize to the SAME JCS bytes and let the shipped signature verify — those two are the reason the check must exist and must be lexical. The runner now executes all four as raw proof bytes rather than reading these fields as claims (round-29 M-1).

rejects.rejectedBy: the JSON parser — it is not a valid JSON number
the JSON parser — it is not a valid JSON number

generationSpelling.whereChecked: Delivery §5a.3, at proof acceptance, before the state is consulted
generationSpelling.whyBothClassesShip: the two that die in the parser show that a conforming reader rejects them anyway; the two that survive to a verifying signature show that nothing downstream can, which is the whole argument for a lexical check at acceptance. Round 28 claimed all four reached JCS and the signature — that was false for 01 and +1 and is corrected here.

stateAtomicity.note: Delivery 4.4/5a.3 — atomicity, executed only where the contract still promises it (round-46 M-1): the one-binding-per-rkid commit of 5a.3 (observable), the queue's declared max-queue-bytes (published constant), and the declared max-binding-tombstones store. Private bounds left the protocol with the 0.65 re-cast and are no longer a conformance subject.

cases.case: two concurrent valid registrations for ONE rkid
tornOrder: A reads: no binding for rkid
B reads: no binding for rkid
cases.why: the rebind commit is a linearizable compare-and-swap: two concurrent valid registrations yield one binding, never two, and never a queue with no authorized collector

cases.case: two concurrent deposits at the queue's declared max-queue-bytes
cases.why: the queue bound is a published constant, so its enforcement is atomic — a counterpart sees the occupancy before or after, never both deposits admitted past it

cases.case: concurrent deadline transitions against one tombstone store
tornOrder: deadline A reads the store (1 of 2 slots free)
deadline B reads the store (sees the same free slot)
cases.why: two deadline transitions racing one store can overfill it or, linearized wrongly, evict the wrong victim — the transition is a check-and-commit like every other bound decision (4.4), and independent deadlines either join one linearized step or serialize

stateAtomicity.rule: every decision against a bound is one linearized check-and-commit: concurrent transitions are joined into one sweep or serialized as separate ones — the interleaving (both read, then both commit) is the torn order every case exhibits and forbids

durationGrammar.note: Round-32 B-2: the six declared durations had no executable grammar — 'RFC 3339 / ISO 8601' names a standard that excludes durations, and windowMs needs whole milliseconds. The grammar is Access §7.3's day/time subset, with no fractional component, so every value maps to an exact integer of milliseconds. Round-34 M-1: the shipped grammar string had kept the older shape (a mandatory day component) while its own accept list contains PT1S — under that reading challenge-lifetime and status-horizon would have had no satisfiable value.
durationGrammar.grammar: P, then an optional <d>D, then an optional T part with <h>H <m>M <s>S in descending order and AT LEAST ONE of the three; at least one component present overall; each value 1-3 digits; no years/months/weeks; no fraction; 1D = 86400 s

reject.why: fractional component — no integer millisecond value, and rounding or truncating would give two conformant readings
months are not in the subset (not fixed-length)
years are not in the subset
weeks are not in the subset
a T that is present carries no component — a bare T is not a value of this grammar (round-35 B-3)

durationGrammar.rejectionRule: a declaration carrying a rejected lexeme is rejected, not rounded and not truncated (4.4, as for every out-of-domain constant)

challengeConsumption.note: Delivery §5a.3 — a challenge is single-use and is consumed by the FIRST response attempt, before that response is verified. A failed verification does not restore it: one issued challenge buys at most one verification, and a fresh attempt begins with a fresh challenge. This is the port-observable half of what used to be the charge machine; the machine itself left the protocol in the 0.65 scope re-cast (a carrier's budgets are its own).

sequence.step: challenge issued for the attacker's own rkid (past the carrier’s own admission decision)
first response arrives: the challenge is consumed, THEN verified — the signature is junk
second response naming the same challenge
sequence.why: nothing live to verify against; discarded at the syntactic step, at the cost of a lookup

sequence.step: a fresh attempt needs a fresh challenge — and a fresh challenge
its first response is verified once

challengeConsumption.invariant: verificationsSoFar never exceeds the number of challenges issued

carrierGuarantees.note: Delivery 4.4 — the five observable guarantees of the 0.65 scope re-cast, each executable. What used to be executed here was the machinery that implemented them; these vectors execute the promises.

rejects.why: a carrier acting on an unpublished bound made identical histories answer differently (round-43 B-2)
an adapter without a declared status horizon can hold a submission silently forever (wot#355)

round-44 B-1 / round-45 M-1: constants for the carrier role declared under any other role URI are not a carrier declaration — without one fixed key, two counterparts could hold different entries as authoritative

behaviour.note: round-48 M-2 — the declaration BINDS: enforcing stricter or looser than published is nonconformant, and status-horizon is executable in time.

sequence.why: a state, not a success — the horizon asks for honesty, not delivery

sequence.event: still no report of any kind
sequence.why: the forty silent minutes of wot#355, caught at the declared horizon

enforcementDrift.why: stricter than published — deposits die 23 days before the declaration says
looser than published — a counterpart planning a return against P90D holds a wrong promise either way: the declaration binds in both directions

g2_precedence_submission.note: round-43 B-3 — overlapping true conditions name ONE verdict: s1 no-such-queue, s2 bounds, s3 duplicate, s4 admission-resource, s5 queue-saturated, s6 capacity. Most specific first.

cases.why: the queue's own bound is more actionable than the carrier's global fill
a wrong address outranks every resource statement
an oversize envelope is judged before any occupancy is consulted
the metering gate is s4, before either occupancy check
the global answer is reachable only when nothing more specific holds

g2_precedence_registration.note: r1 malformed, r2 admission-resource, r3 possession-failed, r4 capacity (under guarantee 4 and the return priority), r5 the state table.

cases.why: r2 runs before any asymmetric verification — guarantee 3 is an ordering rule
r4 before r5: the state table is only consulted for a request the carrier will serve
for a request naming a HELD binding, guarantee 4 removes the r2 refusal when the drain came from unknown-address traffic, so the first condition left standing is the state table's
round-47 M-2: guarantee 4 strikes r2/r4 only when UNKNOWN-address traffic drained the resource — a binding whose own traffic exhausted its budget is DO-6, not starvation, and r2 stands

g3_order.note: guarantee 3 — no randomness, sealing, or asymmetric operation before the decision to serve. The observable half: a refused request has cost the carrier no key operation, so refusals are cheap and unmeterable work cannot be forced by an unauthenticated party.

sequence.why: sealing the address challenge and verifying the signature happen only past the decision

g4_starvation.note: guarantee 4 — traffic for unknown addresses cannot starve a binding the carrier holds, and a return outranks an arrival (5a.9).

sequence.event: flood: requests for unknown rkids exhaust the carrier's own admission budget

sequence.why: a request naming a binding the carrier holds is beyond what unknown-address traffic can exhaust
the return path of a held binding is part of the same guarantee

sequence.event: carrier at its limits: register(new) and register(closing-rkid, g+1) compete
sequence.why: a return outranks an arrival — the refused newcomer lost nothing, the refused returner would have lost a channel

sequence.event: admission meter drained by unknown-address traffic; a valid rebind(held-rkid, g+1) arrives

windUpDeadline.note: 5a.9, recast in 0.66 after round-43 B-1 — the deadline IS the release, one linearized transition. closingBegins fixes the deadline; deposits admitted during closing inherit the remaining time; the deadline transition gives up everything and releases in one step; a return before it ends the wind-up and voids the deadline; a fresh wind-up later gets a FRESH deadline.

sequence.why: admission stays open; the deposit inherits the remaining 600, not a fresh 1000
even one tick before the deadline the queue admits — and the deposit's life ends with the wind-up
give-up of everything held and the release are ONE transition — nothing can slip between them (round-43 B-1)
the return ends the wind-up; held deposits revert to their admission-dated horizons

sequence.event: no collection since the return? then a FRESH orphan-horizon must first pass
sequence.why: closing→live→closing composes only through a full new orphan-horizon and a FRESH deadline — the old instant is void, not paused

postDeadlineReturn.why: a return linearized after the deadline transition meets released(t) and takes the tombstone path — two exchanges, executed in carrierEntryLossRecovery.perHeldState

g2_family.note: round-45 B-2 — the retriable family is closed and split across the two closed sets; WHICH member answers is named by the evaluation orders, never chosen.
